result.answer: No. The calculation does not prove that sqrt(2) is rational; it produces a contradiction from rationality. With the justified choice of a lowest-denominator representation below, the contradiction proves that sqrt(2) is irrational. The original presentation was incomplete unless it supplied the reduction-to-lowest-terms justification.

approaches.description: Use reductio: assume sqrt(2) is rational, select a representation with least positive denominator, prove it has no common factor, then derive that both numerator and denominator are even.
approaches.reason: The least-denominator argument supplies the missing bridge from arbitrary rationality to a lowest-terms representation.

change_log: Replaced the unjustified assumption of a lowest-terms representation with a least-positive-denominator construction.
Added explicit applications of the Well-Ordering Principle and Division Algorithm.
Scoped the temporary assumption as rationality alone and discharged it at the contradiction step.
Revised the conclusion: the argument refutes rationality rather than proves it.

claims.statement: A real number is rational if it equals p/q for integers p,q with q nonzero; it is irrational if it is not rational.

claims.basis_reference: Temporary negation of the desired irrationality conclusion.
claims.statement: Assume temporarily that sqrt(2) is rational.

claims.basis_reference: Derived from the temporary rationality assumption by changing a nonzero denominator to its absolute value if necessary.
claims.statement: There is a nonempty set S of positive integers that occur as denominators in integer representations sqrt(2)=a/b.

claims.basis_reference: Well-Ordering Principle: every nonempty set of positive integers has a least element; applied in step-minimal-denominator to S.
claims.statement: There are integers a and b with b positive, sqrt(2)=a/b, and b least among the positive denominators in S.

claims.basis_reference: A common divisor greater than 1 would produce a smaller positive denominator, contradicting minimality.
claims.statement: The selected integers a and b have no common positive divisor greater than 1.

claims.basis_reference: Derived by squaring sqrt(2)=a/b and multiplying by the nonzero number b^2.
Division Algorithm for divisor 2: every integer n is either 2k or 2k+1 for an integer k; applied in steps step-a-even and step-b-even.
claims.statement: Every integer is even or odd in the form 2k or 2k+1.

claims.basis_reference: If a were odd, its square would be odd, contrary to a^2=2b^2.
claims.statement: There is an integer c such that a=2c.

claims.basis_reference: Substitute a=2c into a^2=2b^2 and cancel 2.
If b were odd, its square would be odd, contrary to b^2=2c^2.
The contradiction discharges the temporary assumption that sqrt(2) is rational.

proof_steps.justification: This fixes the meanings of rational and irrational used in the proof.
proof_steps.statement: A number is rational exactly when it is p/q for integers p,q with q nonzero; irrational means not rational.

proof_steps.justification: This begins a reductio subproof by assuming the negation of irrationality.
proof_steps.statement: Assume sqrt(2)=p/q for some integers p,q with q nonzero.

proof_steps.justification: If q is positive, use p/q; if q is negative, use (-p)/(-q). Thus some positive integer denominator occurs.
proof_steps.statement: Let S be the set of positive integers n for which sqrt(2)=m/n for some integer m; then S is nonempty.

proof_steps.justification: By the Well-Ordering Principle, S has a least element b. By the definition of S, choose an integer a with sqrt(2)=a/b.
proof_steps.statement: Choose b least in S and an integer a such that b>0 and sqrt(2)=a/b.

proof_steps.justification: If a and b had a common positive divisor d>1, write a=da' and b=db' with integers a',b'. Then b'=b/d is a positive integer smaller than b and sqrt(2)=a'/b', so b' is in S, contradicting the minimality of b.
proof_steps.statement: a and b have no common positive divisor greater than 1.

proof_steps.justification: Squaring sqrt(2)=a/b gives 2=a^2/b^2. Since b is positive and hence nonzero, multiplication by b^2 gives a^2=2b^2.
The equation makes a^2 even. By the Division Algorithm for divisor 2, a is 2c or 2c+1. In the latter case, a^2=4c^2+4c+1 is odd; hence a=2c for some integer c.
proof_steps.statement: There is an integer c such that a=2c.

proof_steps.justification: Substitution gives 4c^2=2b^2; cancelling the nonzero integer 2 gives b^2=2c^2.
The equation makes b^2 even. By the Division Algorithm for divisor 2, an odd b would have an odd square, so b is even.
Steps step-a-even and step-b-even show that 2 divides both a and b, contradicting step-lowest-terms. This discharges the temporary assumption in step-assume-rational.
proof_steps.statement: The temporary assumption that sqrt(2) is rational yields a contradiction; therefore sqrt(2) is irrational.
